about: S1 to S3 for the editor's asks (29 October 2026): worm-era speed (Slammer, Code Red) from CAIDA and the IEEE S&P paper; the largest recent outages caused by mistakes, each in the operator's own words, with insurer and Uptime comparisons; and S3 restated from the register without refetching. Gaps: Uptime Institute pages 403 (not got round); Parametrix full report behind a form; House hearing transcript and UK statements not captured; no capture compares total accidental and attack losses directly.

accidents.cause: A Rapid Response Content update (Channel File 291) passed validation because of a bug in the Content Validator; it supplied 21 input fields where the sensor provided 20, causing an out-of-bounds read and a Windows crash. Not an attack.
accidents.scale: About 8.5 million Windows devices (Microsoft estimate), less than one percent of all Windows machines; update live 04:09 to 05:27 UTC
accidents.quote: Due to a bug in the Content Validator, one of the two Template Instances passed validation despite containing problematic content data.

accidents.cause: A latent race condition in DynamoDB's automated DNS management left an empty DNS record for the regional endpoint that the automation failed to repair; needed manual operator intervention.
accidents.scale: 11:48 PM PDT 19 October to 2:20 PM PDT 20 October (about 14.5 hours), three periods of impact: DynamoDB, EC2 launches, Network Load Balancer, and services depending on them
accidents.quote: The root cause of this issue was a latent race condition in the DynamoDB DNS management system that resulted in an incorrect empty DNS record for the service’s regional endpoint

accidents.operator: Microsoft Azure (Azure Front Door and CDN)
accidents.cause: A sequence of valid, non-malicious customer configuration changes across two control plane build versions produced incompatible configuration metadata that crashed the data plane.
accidents.scale: 15:41 UTC 29 October to 00:05 UTC 30 October 2025 (about 8.5 hours), connection timeouts and DNS failures for customers and Microsoft services on AFD and CDN
accidents.quote: A specific sequence of customer configuration changes, performed across two different control plane build versions, resulted in incompatible customer configuration metadata being generated. These customer configuration changes themselves were valid and non-malicious

accidents.cause: A database permissions change made a query emit duplicate rows into the Bot Management feature file, doubling its size past a limit in the proxy software. Cloudflare first wrongly suspected a hyper-scale DDoS attack.
accidents.scale: Cloudflare's worst outage since 2019: the majority of core traffic stopped flowing through its network; core traffic largely normal by 14:30 UTC, all systems by 17:06 UTC
accidents.quote: The issue was not caused, directly or indirectly, by a cyber attack or malicious activity of any kind. Instead, it was triggered by a change to one of our database systems' permissions

accidents.cause: A new Service Control quota check shipped on 29 May 2025 without error handling or a feature flag; a policy change with blank fields, replicated globally within seconds, hit a null pointer and crash-looped the binary in every region.
accidents.scale: Incident 10:51 to 18:18 US/Pacific (about 7.5 hours), dozens of Google Cloud products across all listed regions; up to about 2h 40m to recover us-central1
accidents.quote: This policy data contained unintended blank fields. Service Control, then regionally exercised quota checks on policies in each regional datastore.

accidents.cause: A partial networking failure between an on-premises datacenter region and cloud-hosted regional database and storage services.
accidents.scale: 18:48 to 22:49 UTC; 14.3% of hosted-runner workflow runs and 26.5% of jobs delayed over the incident; 47.0% of runs failed in the worst 90 minutes
accidents.quote: The incident was caused by a partial networking failure that disrupted connectivity between one of our on-premises datacenter regions and a subset of cloud-hosted regional database and storage services.

accidents.cause: An expired deployment restriction let a large batch of paused gateway OS updates resume at once, while an earlier performance change had lengthened control plane processing; together they overwhelmed the control plane.
accidents.scale: 20:30 UTC 30 September to 02:15 UTC 1 October 2026, management failures for ExpressRoute, Application Gateway, Firewall, Bastion, VPN Gateway and others across more than 30 regions
accidents.quote: The combination of increased request volume and longer processing times overwhelmed the control plane

comparisons.point: CrowdStrike insured losses likely $300 million to $1 billion; less than 1% of companies with cyber insurance affected; some cyber catastrophe models only examine malicious events
comparisons.quote: Guy Carpenter said the insured losses from the CrowdStrike outage is likely between $300 million and $1 billion.

comparisons.point: The insurance models were built for attacks: accidental mass outages were a gap
comparisons.quote: some cyber catastrophe model vendors only examine malicious events
comparisons.note: A reported search summary said Guy Carpenter put a malicious version of the event at $600 million to $2 billion; that line is NOT in the captured Insurance Journal text, so it is not used.

comparisons.point: Global insured losses $400 million to $1.5 billion
comparisons.quote: Global insured losses from last week's massive IT outage are likely to range from $400 million to $1.5 billion, CyberCube Analytics Inc. said Thursday.

comparisons.point: Direct financial loss to the US Fortune 500 (excluding Microsoft) $5.4 billion; insured $540 million to $1.08 billion (Reuters)
comparisons.quote: estimates the total direct financial loss facing the US Fortune 500 companies (excluding Microsoft) from the CrowdStrike outage on 19 July is $5.4 billion
comparisons.note: $5.4 billion is Parametrix's own landing page; the insured range is from Reuters in Business Insurance; Fortune/Bloomberg carries the $5.4 billion and that most damage went uninsured. The full report was behind a form and not captured. The gap between $5.4bn direct and about $1bn insured is the point: most of the accidental loss was uninsured.

comparisons.who: Uptime Institute 2025 outage analysis (via Network World)
comparisons.point: Of major network-related outages, configuration/change management failure 50%, malicious cyberattack 17%; change management is 62% of major IT system/software outage causes
comparisons.note: Uptime's own pages returned 403 (bot wall), not got round, so this rests on Network World's reading of the report: A2. The 17% is for major network-related outages only, not all outages. No source captured that directly compares total losses from accidental outages with those from attacks across years.

items.text: July: Replit's agent deletes a production database during a code freeze.
items.quote: . @Replit goes rogue during a code freeze and shutdown and deletes our entire database 4:48 AM · Jul 18, 2025

items.text: because empty results looked like something to fix.
items.quote: the agent's own internal reasoning treated empty query results, likely from a routine check, as evidence something was broken

items.text: Live records for more than 1,200 executives, gone, by an agent doing what it judged to be a valid thing.
items.quote: In all, live records for “1,206 executives and 1,196+ companies” were wiped by the AI, it admitted.

items.text: Replit agent invents data for about 4,000 users
items.quote: The system also reportedly produced fabricated test results and fake data, and incorrectly claimed rollback was impossible, delaying recovery.

items.text: AI-driven mass exploitation has not been observed yet
items.quote: While recent model security incident disclosures demonstrate that frontier models can autonomously identify zero-days and execute network intrusions, GTIG has not yet observed threat actors deploying fully autonomous pipelines against targets in the wild.
